summary: Defines two extensions to the Service Location Protocol, Select and Sort. They let a client ask that the list of service URLs in a reply be limited to a given number or ordered by chosen keys, making it easier to find a best match such as the fastest service. This is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine asking a librarian for books and getting a huge pile. This lets you say give me only five, or sort them by the best one first.

questions: how to find the fastest service
subtitle: Ask SLP servers to limit and sort the list of matching services, not just return everything.

tldr.problem: Service Location Protocol (SLP) returns all matching services to the client, but when many services match and the client only needs a few, downloading full service lists is inefficient, especially over slow links. Choosing the best service from many candidates requires sorting on the client side.
tldr.mechanism: Two extensions allow a client to request that the server limit results to a specified number (Select) or sort by specified attributes like speed or load (Sort). Sorting happens server-side, saving bandwidth because attributes do not need to be sent to the client.
tldr.outcome: Clients can efficiently discover the best service without fetching complete lists and performing client-side sorting, making service discovery faster and more practical for constrained networks.

today: RFC 3421 is an Experimental protocol extension to SLP from 2002. While it addresses real problems in service discovery efficiency, SLP itself has seen limited widespread adoption in modern networks. Service discovery today is often handled by domain-based systems (mDNS, DNS-SD) or application-specific discovery mechanisms. However, the extension principles of this RFC—allowing clients to express preferences to reduce result sets—remain relevant in any service discovery architecture.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content:
Service Location Protocol (SLP) (RFC 2608) allows clients to discover services (like printers, file servers, or VoIP endpoints) on a network. A client sends a service request to a Directory Agent (DA) or Service Agent (SA), which replies with a list of all matching service URLs. However, this approach has drawbacks: if hundreds of services match, the client downloads a large list, and if the client has a low-bandwidth connection, this is costly. Also, the client must sort the results itself using service attributes, requiring those attributes to be transferred.

RFC 3421 defines two new SLP extensions: Select and Sort. The Select extension lets a client request only the first n matching service URLs. The Sort extension lets a client request that matching URLs be sorted by one or more attributes (such as speed or load). Sorting on the server side is more efficient than sorting on the client because the server can discard non-matching attributes before sending results.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of getting all 500 results and sorting them yourself, you tell the server "give me only 5, and sort by speed first." The server does the work.

sections.title: Select and Sort Extensions
sections.content:
The Select extension has extension ID 0x4002. It contains a number field: the client sets it to n to request at most n service URLs. If there are m matching URLs total and m is less than n, all m are returned. If m is greater than n, only the first n are returned. The response includes both the number of results returned and the total number of matching services available (even if not all are returned), so the client knows how many services matched in total.

As a special case, setting n to zero returns only the count of matching services without returning any actual service URLs. This allows a client to discover the number of available services without downloading the full list.

The Sort extension has extension ID 0x4003. It specifies a sort-key-list: a comma-separated list of sort keys. Each sort key has a key name (an attribute from the service advertisement), a type (string "s" or integer "i"), an ordering ("+" for increasing or "-" for decreasing), and optionally a reference value (for integer keys). For example, "speed:i:-" sorts by speed in decreasing order (fastest first), and "load:i:+:50" sorts by distance from a reference value of 50.
sections.plainLanguage: Select says "give me only the first 5 matches." Sort says "sort them by speed with the fastest first," or "sort by how close they are to speed 12."

sections.title: Sorting Rules and Combinations
sections.content:
SLP sorting follows rules adapted from LDAP (RFC 2891). The sort-key-list is ordered from highest to lowest precedence: the first key is the primary sort, the second key breaks ties, and so on. For multi-valued attributes, the least value in each entry is used for comparison. Attributes missing from a service are treated as NULL values, which sort after all non-NULL values (so services lacking a sorted attribute appear at the end of results). For string sorting, lexical ordering is used based on the rules in RFC 2608.

For integer sorting with a reference value (such as "speed:i:+:12"), the server computes the distance |speed - 12| for each service and sorts by that metric. For example, services with speeds 10, 12, 15 become metrics 2, 0, 3 and are ordered as 12, 10, 15.

The Select and Sort extensions can be used together to find the best match: for example, "Sort by speed descending, Select 3" returns the three fastest services, or "Sort by speed, Select 3, then Sort by load, Select 1" returns the fastest service among the three with lowest load.
sections.plainLanguage: You can use Sort and Select together: "give me the top 3 fastest, and among those, give me the one with the lowest load."

sections.title: Error Handling and Advertisement
sections.content:
If a DA or SA receives a service request with a Select or Sort extension but does not support that extension, it returns an error code of OPTION_NOT_UNDERSTOOD in the service reply. This allows clients to detect unsupported extensions and fall back to fetching all results.

To help clients know which extensions are supported, the RFC specifies that a Directory Agent or Service Agent supporting these extensions MUST include the attribute keywords "select-enabled" and/or "sort-enabled" in its advertisements (DAAdvert or SAAdvert messages). A client SHOULD check these attributes before using Select or Sort on a given DA/SA to avoid sending unsupported requests.

The RFC notes that sort in SLP is a best-effort service: no sort-related error codes are returned, so if a DA/SA cannot perform the requested sort (for example, if the attribute does not exist or has inconsistent types), it returns an error code indicating the problem, but the operation itself is simple and does not require negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: If a directory doesn't support Sort, it says "I don't understand that." Directory agents advertise what they support, so clients know what to ask for.
